_note: Plain-language explanations written for BillWise. They are summaries in our own words, not AMA CPT descriptor text. General information only, not medical, legal or financial advice.

terms.title: Billed amount (charge)
terms.text: The billed amount is the provider's full list price for a service, before any insurance discount. It is usually much higher than what anyone actually pays. If you are insured and the provider is in your plan's network, you are normally not responsible for the full billed amount.

terms.title: Allowed amount
terms.text: The allowed amount is the most your health plan recognizes for a service. For in-network providers it is a price the plan and the provider agreed on in advance. The allowed amount is split between what the plan pays and what you owe.

terms.title: Adjustment (contractual discount or write-off)
terms.text: An adjustment is the part of the billed amount the provider agreed to drop because of its contract with your plan. It is usually the billed amount minus the allowed amount. An in-network provider should not bill you for this amount.

terms.title: Insurer paid (plan paid)
terms.text: This is what your health plan actually paid the provider for the service. If it is zero, the most common reasons are that you have not met your deductible yet, the service is not covered, or the claim is still being processed.

terms.title: Patient responsibility (what you owe)
terms.text: Patient responsibility is the part of the allowed amount you are expected to pay. It can be made up of your deductible, coinsurance and copay. On an Explanation of Benefits it is an estimate; the provider sends the actual bill.

terms.title: Deductible
terms.text: A deductible is the amount you pay for covered care each plan year before your plan starts paying its share. Until you meet it, you may owe the whole allowed amount for many services, which is why the plan can show $0.00 paid.

terms.title: Coinsurance
terms.text: Coinsurance is your percentage share of the allowed amount after your deductible is met. For example, with 20% coinsurance on a $100 allowed amount, you owe $20 and the plan pays $80.

terms.title: Copay
terms.text: A copay is a fixed dollar amount you pay for a type of visit or prescription, such as $30 for an office visit. Some plans charge a copay instead of coinsurance for certain services.

terms.title: Out-of-pocket maximum
terms.text: The out-of-pocket maximum is the most you pay for covered, in-network care in a plan year. After you reach it, the plan pays 100% of the allowed amount for covered services for the rest of the year. Premiums do not count toward it.

terms.title: In-network and out-of-network
terms.text: In-network providers have a contract with your plan and accept the allowed amount as full payment. Out-of-network providers have no contract, so the plan may pay less or nothing, and the provider may try to bill you the difference.

terms.title: Balance billing and surprise bills
terms.text: Balance billing is when a provider bills you for the difference between its charge and the allowed amount. Since 2022 the federal No Surprises Act protects most people from surprise balance bills for emergency care and for certain out-of-network care at in-network facilities. If you think a bill breaks these rules, contact your plan or the federal No Surprises Help Desk.

terms.title: Explanation of Benefits (EOB) is not a bill
terms.text: An Explanation of Benefits comes from your health plan and shows how a claim was processed: what was billed, allowed, paid and what you may owe. It is not a bill. Wait for the provider's statement and compare it with the EOB before paying.

terms.title: Possible duplicate charge
terms.text: Two lines with the same date, code and amount may be a billing mistake, though some services really are given twice in one day. Ask the provider for an itemized statement and ask them to confirm or remove the duplicate before you pay.

terms.title: Denied or not covered
terms.text: A denied service is one the plan decided not to pay for. The EOB usually gives a reason code. You can ask the plan to explain the denial and you have the right to appeal it; the deadline is usually listed on the EOB.

terms.title: Pending or unpaid claim
terms.text: If the insurance payment is blank or pending, the plan has not finished processing the claim. The amount shown as your balance may drop once the plan pays, so it is often worth waiting for the EOB before paying.

terms.title: CPT code
terms.text: A CPT code is a five-digit number that describes a medical service or procedure, such as an office visit or a lab test. Providers use these codes to bill insurers. The same code should mean the same service on every bill.

terms.title: HCPCS code
terms.text: A HCPCS Level II code starts with a letter followed by four digits, like J1885. These codes cover things CPT does not, such as drugs given in a clinic, medical supplies and some Medicare services.

terms.title: Modifier
terms.text: A modifier is a two-character add-on to a billing code, such as 25 or RT, that gives extra detail: for example, that a service was separate from another one done the same day, or which side of the body was treated.

terms.title: Itemized statement
terms.text: An itemized statement lists every charge with its date, code and amount. You can ask the provider's billing office for one. It is the best way to check for duplicates, services you did not receive, or errors.

terms.title: Financial assistance and payment plans
terms.text: Nonprofit hospitals in the US are required to have a written financial assistance policy, and many providers offer interest-free payment plans. If a bill is hard to pay, ask the billing office about financial assistance before the account goes to collections.

terms.title: Member ID, account number and claim number
terms.text: The member ID identifies you with your health plan. The account number identifies your account with the provider, and the claim number identifies one claim at the plan. Have these ready when you call, and keep them private like other personal information.

codes.title: Office visit, established patient (lower level)
codes.text: A routine office visit with a provider who has seen you in the past three years, for a fairly simple problem. It is one of the most common visit codes.

codes.title: Office visit, established patient (moderate level)
codes.text: An office visit with a provider who has seen you before, for a problem that took a moderate amount of medical decision-making, such as managing a chronic condition or adjusting medications.

codes.title: Office visit, new patient (lower level)
codes.text: A first visit with a provider or practice that has not seen you in the past three years, for a fairly simple problem.

codes.title: Emergency department visit (highest level)
codes.text: The highest of the five emergency department visit levels, used when the problem required complex decision-making. It covers the emergency physician's evaluation; tests, scans and medicines are billed separately.

codes.title: Emergency department visit (middle level)
codes.text: The middle of the five emergency department visit levels. It covers the emergency physician's evaluation; tests, scans and medicines are billed separately.

codes.title: Comprehensive metabolic panel (blood test)
codes.text: A common blood test that checks a group of chemicals in your blood, including sugar, electrolytes, and markers of kidney and liver function.

codes.title: Complete blood count with differential (blood test)
codes.text: A blood test that counts red cells, white cells and platelets, and breaks the white cells down by type. It is used to look for infection, anemia and other conditions.

codes.title: Blood draw (venipuncture)
codes.text: The charge for drawing blood from a vein with a needle. The lab tests run on the blood are billed under their own codes.

codes.title: Chest X-ray, two views
codes.text: An X-ray of the chest taken from two angles, often used to check the lungs and heart, for example for pneumonia.

codes.title: Electrocardiogram (ECG/EKG) with reading
codes.text: A recording of the heart's electrical activity using stickers on the chest, including the provider's reading and report of the results.

codes.title: CT scan of abdomen and pelvis with contrast
codes.text: A detailed cross-sectional X-ray scan of the belly and pelvis, taken after a contrast dye is given to make organs and blood vessels show up more clearly.

codes.title: CT scan of the head without contrast
codes.text: A detailed X-ray scan of the head or brain taken without contrast dye, often used after a head injury or for sudden symptoms like a severe headache.

codes.title: Urinalysis with microscope check
codes.text: A urine test done by machine that also includes looking at the sample under a microscope, often used to check for infection or kidney problems.

codes.title: IV push of a medicine (first or only drug)
codes.text: The charge for giving a medicine quickly through an IV line. The medicine itself is billed separately, often with a J code.

codes.title: Ketorolac injection (per 15 mg)
codes.text: An injection of ketorolac (often known by the brand name Toradol), a strong anti-inflammatory pain reliever. The code is billed per 15 mg, so a larger dose can appear as more than one unit.

codes.title: Ondansetron injection (per 1 mg)
codes.text: An injection of ondansetron (often known by the brand name Zofran), a medicine for nausea and vomiting. The code is billed per 1 mg, so a typical dose appears as several units.

codes.title: Miscellaneous surgical supply
codes.text: A catch-all code for a surgical supply that has no specific code of its own. Because it is vague, it is reasonable to ask the provider exactly what supply this was.

codes.title: Vaccine administration (first vaccine)
codes.text: The charge for giving a vaccine by injection. The vaccine itself is billed under a separate code.

codes.title: Flu vaccine (the vaccine itself)
codes.text: The cost of a dose of a four-strain flu vaccine without preservatives. The charge for giving the shot is billed separately, often as 90471.

codes.title: Therapeutic exercise (per 15 minutes)
codes.text: Physical therapy exercises to build strength, range of motion or flexibility, billed in 15-minute units. Several units may appear for one session.

codes.title: Medicare annual wellness visit (follow-up year)
codes.text: A yearly Medicare visit to update your prevention plan and health risk review. It is not a full physical exam; if a problem is also treated at the same visit, a separate office visit code may appear.

codes.title: Rapid strep test
codes.text: A quick swab test of the throat for the bacteria that cause strep throat, with results in minutes.
